I know that these things change over time, but the defining characteristic of liberalism since its inception has been to pursue more liberty for more people. In the early days, this meant opposing systems of government that had an astonishing level of control over the details of individual people's lives, so early forms of liberalism look like what we call "libertarianism" today: Individual rights and autonomy as a central belief, along with a push for less government control over commerce and the daily lives of the governed people.

The kind of liberal that is more common today, the much-maligned "welfare liberal" is still a spiritual descendant of that school of thought. After a few hundred years of this individual liberty and property rights and the power of capitalism, there was a growing awareness that government control isn't the only opponent of individual liberty. Extreme income equality leads to a situation where the lives of the poor are controlled not by their desires, but by their basic human needs. Little Billy can't very well be the next great scientist if he has to drop out of school early to help his family pay rent and feed themselves, while some rich idiot gets a free ride through a University education that they don't give a fuck about.

These two ideologies are both liberal, and it does a disservice to try to claim that one or the other isn't. I think the greatest irony is that if you boil it down, conservatism is just about not shaking things up in society too quickly, and even though conservatives way back when would have opposed liberals, conservatives today end up praising the old liberal ideals because they've been around long enough that our society has adapted to them.
